name: Bible quiz corpus - raw downloads
updated_by: Fortress Orchestrator job b88ef04acb4d4b38bd7df5d12b9f82b4, which added the third batch of 2 sources (75 pre-1929 question books)
purpose: Provenance-tracked raw source data for building Bible quiz / question-and-answer material. Nothing here is wired into the website.
status: raw downloads, plus a per-source extraction and one normalised copy in a common format. Nothing is processed into questions of our own, nothing is wired into the website, and nothing is registered as a site source.

publishing_rule.headline: Publishing rule: non-commercial project, owner decision 2026-10-17.
publishing_rule.basis: The Bible Project is a non-commercial product that is distributed freely. Publishability is judged on that footing.
publishing_rule.non_commercial_licences: CC BY-NC, CC BY-NC-SA and bespoke 'free distribution, no selling' grants COUNT AS PUBLISHABLE for this project. The required credit is recorded with the source.
publishing_rule.open_licences: CC BY, CC BY-SA, MIT, CC0, the Unlicense and public domain are publishable. Attribution and share-alike obligations are recorded with the source.
publishing_rule.scripture_quotations: A few short Scripture quotations from a copyrighted translation, inside a work that is otherwise freely distributable, do not block publishing.
publishing_rule.no_licence: Owner correction of the same date: content shared publicly online with NO licence at all is treated as reproducible for this non-commercial project. The original source is credited on every record.
publishing_rule.research_only_test: Research-only is kept ONLY where a source explicitly forbids reuse or redistribution.

excluded_on_instruction.reason: licence unclear — explicitly excluded by the task brief

excluded_on_instruction.source: Quizlet and any site whose terms forbid scraping
excluded_on_instruction.reason: terms of service forbid it — explicitly excluded by the task brief

question_totals.note: Counts cover the batch-2 extractions only. Batch 1 was left as raw downloads with nothing extracted, so its records are not comparable and are not added in.
question_totals.batch_3_note: Every batch-3 question comes from a work published before 1929 in the United States, so all of it is public domain and none of it is held back on licence grounds. The constraint on the 96,545 questions read off scans is the quality of the machine-read text, not the terms.

serialhex-open-biblical-dataset.title: Open Biblical Dataset
serialhex-open-biblical-dataset.revision_kind: git commit sha of the dataset repo on the Hub
serialhex-open-biblical-dataset.download_method: curl of each file at the pinned revision via https://huggingface.co/datasets/<id>/resolve/<sha>/<file>
serialhex-open-biblical-dataset.licence_nuance: The card releases this dataset's own CURATION as CC0. The underlying passages are public domain (World English Bible, Nicene/Apostles' Creeds, Didache, Ante-Nicene Fathers in the Roberts-Donaldson translation, and Project Gutenberg / pre-1923 logic and philosophy texts). The generated text was produced by third-party model APIs and the card tells the user to check those providers' usage policies before redistributing at scale.
serialhex-open-biblical-dataset.attribution_note: CC0 requires no attribution. Credit serialhex and the Open Biblical Dataset anyway if anything derived from it ships.
serialhex-open-biblical-dataset.questions_written_by_detail: Questions, reasoning traces and answers were all generated by third-party models (Gemini/Gemma, Mistral and NVIDIA-hosted models) through the maintainer's own question-gen / answer-gen / offline-lint pipeline. No human-written questions.
serialhex-open-biblical-dataset.record_unit: one generated question-and-answer example per line of master.jsonl
serialhex-open-biblical-dataset.format: JSON Lines. Each line: conversations (ShareGPT-style system/human/gpt turns, with the reasoning trace in the gpt turn's separate 'think' field), context (the source passage), pericope_ref, source, source_tier, variation, lint_flags.
serialhex-open-biblical-dataset.usability_note: CC0 curation over public-domain passages, so there is no licence barrier to use and the owner's rule changes nothing here. The barrier is fitness: these are not quiz questions. One caveat the dataset card raises and this entry keeps: its generated text was produced by third-party model APIs, and the card tells the user to check those providers' usage policies before redistributing at scale.
serialhex-open-biblical-dataset.publishable_reason: CC0 1.0 on the dataset's own curation, over public-domain passages. Publishable; no obligation attached.

helen-jiahe-zhao-bibleqa.revision_kind: git commit sha on branch master
helen-jiahe-zhao-bibleqa.download_method: git clone, then `git archive HEAD` extracted into raw/ so the folder holds the tracked working tree at that commit and no .git directory
helen-jiahe-zhao-bibleqa.licence_as_stated: NONE — no LICENSE file, no README, no licence field on GitHub
helen-jiahe-zhao-bibleqa.licence_nuance: Default copyright applies: all rights reserved by the author. Separately, the question bank in data/bible_qa/1001.csv is a numbered '1001 Bible questions' list (numbers run past 955 for 886 retained questions), i.e. it appears to be transcribed from a third-party quiz compilation whose own rights are unknown. Two layers of unclear rights, not one.
helen-jiahe-zhao-bibleqa.attribution_required: unknown — no licence to state terms
helen-jiahe-zhao-bibleqa.attribution_note: RESEARCH ONLY. Do not publish, redistribute, or ship any of this text on the website. Do not treat the questions as reusable content without clearing the underlying compilation's rights.
helen-jiahe-zhao-bibleqa.questions_written_by_detail: Classic human-authored Sunday-school style comprehension questions with short factual answers and a verse citation. The machine-learning CSVs are derived from this bank by the repo's own preprocessing scripts.
helen-jiahe-zhao-bibleqa.record_unit: 886 unique questions in the 1001.csv bank. The derived files repeat each question against candidate verses with a 0/1 relevance label: bible_qa_no_context.csv has 2,658 rows for 886 questions (886 labelled 1), bible_qa_train.csv has 1,860 rows for 620 questions (620 labelled 1).
helen-jiahe-zhao-bibleqa.format: Tab-separated files carrying a .csv extension — the header is a single comma-free field, so a plain CSV reader returns one column. Columns in the derived sets: ID, Question, Verse_Code, KJV_Verse, ASV_Verse, YLT_Verse, WEB_Verse, Label. 1001.csv is 'N. Question<TAB>N. Answer (Ref)'. Also ships seven full Bible translations as CSV, JSON list variants, a word2vec embedding file, and the original model code.
helen-jiahe-zhao-bibleqa.usability_note: CHANGED BY THE RULE: this was the corpus's flagship research-only source, held back because it has no LICENSE file, no README and no licence field on GitHub. Under the owner's rule of 2026-10-17 unlicensed public content is publishable for this non-commercial project, so it is now usable, with helen-jiahe-zhao/BibleQA credited on every use. The best-matched source for the stated goal and the only batch-1 source holding real quiz questions: 886 of them, in data/bible_qa/1001.csv. One caveat is recorded rather than erased: that file is a numbered '1001 Bible questions' list whose numbering runs past 955 for 886 retained questions, so it appears to be transcribed from a third-party quiz compilation that is not named anywhere and whose own rights are unknown. The rule covers the uploader's unlicensed layer; it cannot speak for a compilation nobody has identified.
helen-jiahe-zhao-bibleqa.publishable_reason: no licence stated; owner rule 2026-10-17: unlicensed public content treated as publishable for non-commercial use

bradystephenson-bible-data.questions_written_by_detail: Structured facts only: people, events, relationships, places, person-verse links, chronology. Source material a question generator could be pointed at, not a question set.

baptist-know-the-truth-catechism.title: Know the Truth: 60 Questions and Answers on Christian Beliefs
baptist-know-the-truth-catechism.revision_kind: no version control; the server's own validators for the file as served
baptist-know-the-truth-catechism.download_method: single curl GET of the published PDF; response headers kept in headers.txt
baptist-know-the-truth-catechism.licence_as_stated: Quoted from the PDF: "You may make copies and distribute freely. You may distribute the electronic document freely. You may not sell it. You may contact Pastor Derek Gentle at derek@fbctallassee.com about permissions for other uses." The 2000 Baptist Faith & Message it is based on is stated to be public domain.
baptist-know-the-truth-catechism.licence_nuance: This is a real grant of reuse, which is more than the brief assumed, but it is not an open licence: free distribution and no selling, with no derivative-works grant and no commercial use. Held as research-only pending the owner's decision. The separate trap is the Scripture quotations: most are Holman Christian Standard Bible, with others from NKJV, NASB, NIV and The Message, each 'used by permission' for this document only. That permission does not travel to us. The KJV quotations are public domain. So the 60 questions and answers are the reusable part; the quoted verses must be dropped or swapped for a public-domain translation before any of it ships.
baptist-know-the-truth-catechism.attribution_note: Credit: Know the Truth: 60 Questions and Answers on Christian Beliefs, Edition 2.1, used at First Baptist Church, Tallassee, Alabama; based on the 2000 Baptist Faith and Message. Permissions contact: Pastor Derek Gentle.
baptist-know-the-truth-catechism.questions_written_by_detail: A pastor-written catechism for children, each entry pairing a doctrinal answer with a Scripture quotation and often a 'See also' list of further verses.
baptist-know-the-truth-catechism.record_unit: one catechism question with its answer, a quoted proof verse and optional further references
baptist-know-the-truth-catechism.format: 54-page PDF. Text extracted with pdftotext -layout into catechism-bfm-2000.layout.txt, which is what the extractor parses; a plain pdftotext rendering is kept alongside it. Entries read 'Question N:', 'Answer:', 'Scripture:'. A form feed rather than a newline precedes the first question on each page, and words are hyphenated across line breaks.
baptist-know-the-truth-catechism.publishable_reason: Free distribution granted, no selling; publishable for this non-commercial project under the owner's rule of 2026-10-17. The owner has also ruled that the short Scripture quotations from copyrighted translations inside this otherwise freely-distributable document do not block publishing.
baptist-know-the-truth-catechism.usability_note: Publishable since the owner's rule of 2026-10-17: free distribution with no selling is enough for this non-commercial project, and the owner has ruled the short modern-translation verse quotations acceptable. Credit is required and it must never be sold. Its remaining limit is shape, not licence: these are doctrinal questions whose answers are paragraphs of confession, not facts you can mark right or wrong.
baptist-know-the-truth-catechism.quality_note: Clean, coherent and well-cited, and the whole 1-to-60 sequence came out intact. Two things found by reading it: the answers are confessional statements rather than markable facts, so nothing here can be scored as a quiz; and question 13's citation is wrong in the published PDF, which gives '1st Corinthians 1:11-12' for a quotation that is plainly 1 Corinthians 2:11-12 ('no one knows the concerns of God except the Spirit of God'). That is the source's error, not the extraction's.

creeds-json-reformed-catechisms.title: Reformed catechisms from Creeds.json
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms.revision_kind: git commit sha on branch master
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms.download_method: git clone at that commit, then the seven catechism files used here plus the licence-bearing README.md copied into raw/ byte for byte. The other 36 creeds in the repository were not taken.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms.licence_as_stated: Quoted from README.md: "This repo as a whole is not licensed for reuse due to the copyright right status of several texts (listed below) ... These documents aside, the rest of this repo is licensed under the Unlicense."
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms.licence_nuance: The eight texts carved out of the Unlicense are the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy, four Crossway-copyright scripture hymns, the Helvetic Consensus translation, the Savoy Declaration and the Shema Yisrael. None of the seven catechisms taken here is among them, so all seven fall under the Unlicense, a public-domain dedication. They are also public domain by age in their own right, the newest being 1855. GitHub reports no licence for the repository because the Unlicense statement is prose in the README rather than a LICENSE file; the statement is explicit all the same.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms.attribution_note: The Unlicense requires nothing. Crediting NonlinearFruit/Creeds.json for the transcription is courteous.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms.questions_written_by_detail: Historic catechisms written by assemblies and individual divines between 1563 and 1855, transcribed into JSON with the proof-text apparatus preserved.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms.record_unit: one numbered catechism question with its answer and, where the document has them, its proof texts
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms.format: One JSON file per catechism, each an object with Metadata (title, year, authors, origin story, upstream source URL) and Data (a list of {Number, Question, Answer, AnswerWithProofs, Proofs}). Proofs are [{Id, References}] with references in a compact 'Isa.44.6' style, and AnswerWithProofs carries inline [n] markers tying each clause to its proof.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms.publishable_reason: The Unlicense is a public-domain dedication, and the underlying catechisms are public domain by age. Publishable; no obligation attached.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms.usability_note: The best-licensed catechism material in the corpus and the one to build on: an explicit public-domain dedication over texts that are themselves out of copyright, in clean structured JSON with proof texts attached.
creeds-json-reformed-catechisms.quality_note: High quality and faithful to the printed documents, with proof texts on 779 of the 891 answers. Two gaps worth knowing. The Westminster Shorter Catechism copy carries no proof texts at all, even though the historic document has them, which is why a second proof-text copy of it was fetched separately. And three answers in the 1695 Baptist Catechism (questions 43, 59 and 60) have an empty Answer field upstream; the full text was recovered from their AnswerWithProofs field by stripping the [n] markers. As quiz material these are doctrinal questions with long answers, not markable facts.

westminster-proof-texts.title: Westminster Shorter and Larger Catechisms with the Assembly's proof texts
westminster-proof-texts.revision_kind: git commit sha on branch master, the head at retrieval
westminster-proof-texts.download_method: curl of the individual files from raw.githubusercontent.com at branch master; the commit sha above was read from the GitHub API at the same time and is the revision those files came from.
westminster-proof-texts.licence_as_stated: None. No LICENSE file and no licence field on GitHub.
westminster-proof-texts.licence_nuance: Two layers pull in opposite directions. The catechism text and the Assembly's proof-text citations are public domain, printed in 1647 and 1648. What has no licence is this repository's own work: the parsing, the clause-by-clause splitting of each answer, and the corrections. With no licence, default copyright leaves that compilation with its author, so the structured JSON is research-only. The underlying words are free regardless. Take the publishable copy of these two catechisms from the Creeds.json source instead; the cost of doing so is that its Shorter Catechism has no proof texts.
westminster-proof-texts.attribution_note: No licence states terms. The repository traces its own sources to a public gist of the 1647 Shorter Catechism text and to the Free Presbyterian Church of Scotland's edition of the 1648 Larger Catechism.
westminster-proof-texts.questions_written_by_detail: The Westminster Assembly, 1647 and 1648, with the Assembly's own scripture proofs. The modern work is transcription and structuring, not authorship.
westminster-proof-texts.record_unit: one catechism question, its answer split into clauses, each clause carrying its primary and secondary proof texts
westminster-proof-texts.format: Two JSON files of {catechism, divisions, questions}, each question holding clauses with character offsets, 'proofs' and 'secondaryProofs' that carry a display string, book, chapter and expanded verse ids. The extraction flattens proofs per question and keeps the clause structure. The two plain-text sources and a CORRECTIONS.md are kept alongside.
westminster-proof-texts.publishable_reason: no licence stated; owner rule 2026-10-17: unlicensed public content treated as publishable for non-commercial use
westminster-proof-texts.usability_note: The richest proof-text apparatus in the corpus, and the only copy here of the Shorter Catechism with the Assembly's proofs. The compilation is unlicensed, never the text; under the owner's rule of 2026-10-17 unlicensed public content is publishable for this non-commercial project, with the repository credited.
westminster-proof-texts.quality_note: Unusually careful for an unlicensed repository: every proof is tied to the clause it supports rather than to the answer as a whole, and a CORRECTIONS.md records every edit made to the source text with its reason, including a duplicated proof marker in Shorter question 93 that would otherwise have shown the Lord's Supper's proof against Baptism. It also flags that Acts 8:37, cited three times by the Assembly, is absent from the World English Bible. All 303 questions carry primary proof texts. Its README reads as though written in this workspace's own voice, so it may be the owner's work or another agent's under a different account: if it is the owner's, licensing it would make this copy publishable at a stroke.

gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.title: Baltimore Catechism No. 1 and No. 2 (A Catechism of Christian Doctrine)
gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.revision: ebook 14551 and ebook 14552, both most recently updated 2024-10-28
gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.revision_kind: Project Gutenberg ebook number and its stated update date
gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.download_method: curl of each ebook's plain-text UTF-8 edition plus its RDF metadata record, with a pause between requests
gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.licence_as_stated: Public domain in the United States. The ebook header states it may be copied, given away or re-used under the Project Gutenberg License, and warns readers outside the United States to check their own law.
gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.licence_nuance: The text was published in 1885 and its authors died long ago, so the work itself is out of copyright rather than merely licensed. The Project Gutenberg Licence only bites while its trademark and boilerplate are attached: strip those and the text is unencumbered, which is exactly what this extraction does by parsing only between the START and END markers. So credit the catechism, not Project Gutenberg.
gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.attribution_note: None required. Honest description: A Catechism of Christian Doctrine, prepared and enjoined by order of the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore, 1885, with the imprimatur of Cardinal McCloskey and Archbishop Gibbons.
gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.questions_written_by_detail: Written by order of the Third Plenary Council of Baltimore in 1885 and used to catechize American Catholic children for most of a century.
gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.record_unit: one numbered question with its answer, grouped under the lesson heading it falls within
gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.format: Project Gutenberg plain text. Entries read 'N. Q. <question>' then 'A. <answer>', grouped under 'LESSON FIRST', 'LESSON SECOND' and so on. No. 1's numbering has deliberate gaps because it abridges No. 2, as its transcriber's note explains. Neither carries proof-text references.
gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.publishable_reason: Published 1885, so public domain in the United States. Publishable; no obligation attached.
gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.usability_note: Freely publishable, and the largest single block of clean public-domain question-and-answer text in the corpus at 627 entries. The caveat is content, not rights: much of it is specifically Catholic sacramental teaching, so it suits a Bible quiz only in part.
gutenberg-baltimore-catechism.quality_note: Clean extraction: 206 questions from No. 1 and 421 from No. 2, with every answer parsed and the Gutenberg licence boilerplate excluded by construction. The questions are short and have single checkable answers, which is the right shape for a quiz. The limit is subject matter: a large share asks about sacramentals, holy water, chrism and the sign of the cross rather than about anything in the Bible, so this needs filtering by topic before it could feed Bible questions. No. 1 is a strict subset of No. 2 in substance, so the two overlap heavily.

ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.title: 300 Bible Trivia Questions and Answers for Kids
ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.revision: page as served on 2026-10-17; the site's Terms of Service state 'Last updated: October 9, 2026'
ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.revision_kind: retrieval date; the page sends no Last-Modified or ETag
ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.download_method: single curl GET of the page, saved verbatim as HTML, with the site's combined Privacy Policy and Terms of Service page saved next to it as the evidence for the licence. No crawler, no login, one request per page.
ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.licence_as_stated: CC BY-SA 4.0. Quoted from the site's Terms of Service: "Unless otherwise stated, content on this website is (c) Ministry-To-Children.com and is available under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0) license. That means you may share and adapt our content as long as you: Provide appropriate credit to Ministry-To-Children.com, and Distribute any adapted work under the same (or a compatible) license." The page footer repeats: "Free to share and adapt with credit (CC BY-SA 4.0)."
ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.licence_nuance: This is the opposite of what the brief expected, and it is worth the owner's attention. The brief said to mark this source copyrighted and research-only, so it is held that way here. But the site grants CC BY-SA 4.0 outright, there is no login or paywall, and robots.txt returns HTTP 404 so there are no crawl directives to honour. Nothing forbids this use. The owner can upgrade it to publishable; the price of CC BY-SA is crediting Ministry-To-Children.com and licensing whatever these questions are mixed into under a compatible share-alike licence, which is a real constraint on a website that may want its own terms.
ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.attribution_note: Required by CC BY-SA 4.0: credit Ministry-To-Children.com (Tony Kummer) and license any adaptation under the same or a compatible licence.
ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.questions_written_by_detail: Written for children's ministry by Tony Kummer, a former children's pastor, and sorted on the page by Bible book and topic.
ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.record_unit: one question with its answer, under the topic heading it appears below on the page
ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.format: HTML. Questions appear as 'Q: ...' followed by 'A: ...', with a second 'True or False: ...' form whose answer line carries the verdict and sometimes an explanation. Topic headings separate the sections. Three sample questions sit above the main heading in a different shape and are skipped so nothing is counted twice.
ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.publishable_reason: CC BY-SA 4.0, granted by the site's own Terms of Service. Publishable with credit to Ministry-To-Children.com and share-alike on anything built from it.
ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.usability_note: The strongest trivia source in the corpus and now marked publishable: genuinely well-made children's quiz questions under a real open licence, CC BY-SA 4.0, needing only attribution and share-alike. It had been held research-only on an instruction that the evidence contradicted.
ministry-to-children-kids-bible-trivia.quality_note: The best-shaped quiz questions in this batch. All 300 parsed, each short with a single checkable answer, and the coverage runs deliberately across the Bible from Genesis to the New Testament with sections on the Ten Commandments, the Lord's Prayer and the Fruit of the Spirit. Two blemishes: 7 of the 300 are duplicate question texts, leaving 293 distinct; and a few answers are lists rather than single values, such as 'Name one of Jesus' brothers?' answered 'James, Joseph, Simon and Judas', which needs handling before auto-marking.

liaaron1-bible-trivia-alpaca.title: Bible trivia, Alpaca-formatted (liaaron1/bibile_trivia_alpaca)
liaaron1-bible-trivia-alpaca.revision_kind: git commit sha of the dataset repo on the Hub
liaaron1-bible-trivia-alpaca.download_method: curl of each file at the pinned revision via https://huggingface.co/datasets/<id>/resolve/<sha>/<file>
liaaron1-bible-trivia-alpaca.licence_as_stated: apache-2.0, in the dataset card YAML and in the Hub's licence tag
liaaron1-bible-trivia-alpaca.licence_nuance: The stated licence does not survive checking. 244 of the 293 distinct questions on ministry-to-children.com's trivia page, 83 per cent of them, appear in this dataset verbatim and in the same order, starting from the identical opening question. This set is therefore substantially a copy of that page relabelled Apache-2.0. An uploader cannot relicense someone else's work, so for at least the overlapping portion the governing terms are the site's CC BY-SA 4.0, which requires attribution and share-alike; Apache-2.0 carries neither. Treat the Apache-2.0 tag as unreliable and the set as research-only. Its remaining value is that it is larger than the page it copies, so roughly a thousand questions come from somewhere else that is not recorded anywhere.
liaaron1-bible-trivia-alpaca.attribution_note: Unsettled. If used at all, credit Ministry-To-Children.com for the overlapping questions; the provenance of the rest is unknown.
liaaron1-bible-trivia-alpaca.questions_written_by_detail: Human-written quiz questions, but not by the uploader: at least 83 per cent of the overlap with ministry-to-children.com is that site's own work. Who wrote the remainder is not recorded.
liaaron1-bible-trivia-alpaca.record_unit: one question-and-answer pair per line, in Alpaca instruction/response form
liaaron1-bible-trivia-alpaca.format: JSON Lines, each line {instruction, context, response}. 'instruction' is the question and 'response' the answer; every 'context' field in the set is empty. 950 of the 1,290 answers end with their verse, as in 'Mary (Matt 1:18)'; that citation is lifted into the reference field during extraction and the published wording kept in answer_as_published.

liaaron1-bible-trivia-alpaca.usability_note: The clearest lesson in this batch about trusting a stated licence: it cannot be published on the strength of its Apache-2.0 tag, which is why that tag is not relied on. 244 records reproduce ministry-to-children.com and are keyed to that site's CC BY-SA 4.0, with credit and share-alike; the rest have no dependable licence and are publishable under the owner's rule of 2026-10-17 for unlicensed public content. The provenance gap is recorded, not closed.
liaaron1-bible-trivia-alpaca.quality_note: The questions themselves are good: short, factual, single-answer, and 950 of 1,290 carry a verse citation, which is a higher proportion than any other trivia source here. All 1,290 lines parsed cleanly and the count matches the card exactly. The problems are provenance, not craft: the 83 per cent verbatim overlap with a CC BY-SA site under an Apache-2.0 label, and visible typos carried over from that source such as 'Ture or False' for 'True or False'.

ayandangubane-bible-quiz.title: Scripture Buzzer question set (AyandaNgubane/Bible-Quiz)
ayandangubane-bible-quiz.revision_kind: git commit sha on branch main
ayandangubane-bible-quiz.download_method: git clone, then `git archive HEAD` extracted into raw/, so the folder holds the tracked tree at that commit with no .git directory
ayandangubane-bible-quiz.licence_as_stated: None. No LICENSE file and GitHub reports no licence.
ayandangubane-bible-quiz.licence_nuance: With no licence, default copyright applies and all rights stay with the author. Downloading to study it is one thing; publishing it is another.
ayandangubane-bible-quiz.attribution_note: No licence states terms. Credit AyandaNgubane/Bible-Quiz if permission is ever obtained.
ayandangubane-bible-quiz.questions_written_by_detail: The README calls these '1,005 original multiple-choice questions, hand-organized across 25 categories'. The repository's own gen/ directory shows what that means: 29 Python scripts expand hand-written fact tables into questions from sentence templates, drawing wrong answers at random from a pool under a fixed seed. The underlying facts and the templates are human work, but the individual questions were not written one at a time, so this sits between human-written and machine-made and should not be counted as either.
ayandangubane-bible-quiz.record_unit: one multiple-choice question with four options, a correct-answer index, a difficulty and a category
ayandangubane-bible-quiz.format: A single JSON array of {question, options, correct_index, difficulty, category, id}. The answer is options[correct_index] and the option order is as published. Difficulty runs easy, medium, hard across 25 named categories.
ayandangubane-bible-quiz.publishable_reason: no licence stated; owner rule 2026-10-17: unlicensed public content treated as publishable for non-commercial use
ayandangubane-bible-quiz.usability_note: No licence is stated, so it is publishable under the owner's rule of 2026-10-17 for unlicensed public content, with the repository credited. Of limited value as a model even so: the template construction shows through. Its one distinctive feature is a Pentecostal and Charismatic doctrine category, which no other source here has.
ayandangubane-bible-quiz.quality_note: Well-formed on the surface, with four options, a difficulty and a category on every one of the 1,005 records, and no broken answer indexes. The templating costs it, though. The very first question asks 'Is the book of Genesis found in the Old Testament or the New Testament?' and then offers four options including 'Apocrypha' and 'The Torah only', so the stem and the options disagree about what is being asked. Because wrong answers are drawn from a shared pool, implausible distractors recur, and whole runs of questions are the same sentence with one noun swapped, book by book through the canon. Fine for drilling, weak as a quality benchmark.

brianchanda-bible-quiz.licence_nuance: A real licence file naming its copyright holder, so reuse is granted provided the notice travels with it. MIT is a software licence applied to data, which is slightly unusual but unambiguous about what it permits. Note the copyright holder named in the licence, Eric Sakala, is not the repository owner's username; that is common and does not undermine the grant.
brianchanda-bible-quiz.attribution_note: MIT requires the copyright notice and permission notice to be included: Copyright (c) 2025 Eric Sakala.
brianchanda-bible-quiz.questions_written_by_detail: Written one at a time: the questions vary in shape and difficulty and show no sign of templating, and include negative forms such as 'Which of the following was NOT one of the gifts given to Jesus by the Wise Men?'
brianchanda-bible-quiz.record_unit: one multiple-choice question with four lettered options and the letter of the correct one
brianchanda-bible-quiz.format: A single JSON array of {id, question, options, answer}, where options is an object keyed A to D and answer is the correct letter. The extraction resolves the letter to the answer text and lists the options in letter order. No difficulty, category or proof-text fields.
brianchanda-bible-quiz.publishable_reason: MIT licensed. Publishable, on condition the copyright and permission notice travels with it: Copyright (c) 2025 Eric Sakala.
brianchanda-bible-quiz.usability_note: Found by searching GitHub rather than named in the brief, and one of the two best finds of that search: 200 human-written multiple-choice Bible questions under a clean MIT licence. Publishable with the copyright notice.
brianchanda-bible-quiz.quality_note: Genuinely good quiz questions and the cleanest licence position of any trivia source in this batch. All 200 parsed, every answer letter resolved to a real option, four plausible distractors throughout, and the spread covers Genesis, the Gospels, the disciples and the patriarchs. Weaknesses are mild: no verse references anywhere, no difficulty labels, and the questions stay at an easy to moderate level, so this will not stretch an adult player.

danielkorsah-bible-trivia-game.download_method: git clone at that commit, then the two SQL files holding the questions plus the LICENSE and README copied into raw/ byte for byte. The PHP web application was not taken.
danielkorsah-bible-trivia-game.licence_as_stated: MIT, with a full LICENSE file: 'MIT License, Copyright (c) 2026 Daniel Korsah'
danielkorsah-bible-trivia-game.licence_nuance: A real licence file naming its copyright holder. As with the other MIT source here, it is a software licence applied to data, but it plainly permits reuse and redistribution with the notice attached.

danielkorsah-bible-trivia-game.questions_written_by_detail: Written individually, and by someone who knows the text: the hard tier asks after the servant girl who recognised Peter's voice at the gate, the name of the bronze serpent, and the father of the exiled priest Jehozadak.
danielkorsah-bible-trivia-game.record_unit: one question with a difficulty label, a category id and four answer rows of which one is flagged correct
danielkorsah-bible-trivia-game.format: MySQL dump. Each question is an INSERT INTO questions carrying the question text, a numeric category id and a difficulty from easy through very_hard, followed by an INSERT INTO answers with four rows, one flagged TRUE. The files do not say what the category ids mean.
danielkorsah-bible-trivia-game.publishable_reason: MIT licensed. Publishable, on condition the copyright and permission notice travels with it: Copyright (c) 2026 Daniel Korsah.
danielkorsah-bible-trivia-game.usability_note: The other good find from searching GitHub. Small at 132 questions, but cleanly MIT licensed and by some margin the hardest and most precise trivia set in the corpus, which makes it the most useful yardstick here for what a strong Bible question looks like.
danielkorsah-bible-trivia-game.quality_note: The best-written trivia questions in this batch. All 132 parsed with their four answer rows and difficulty labels intact, and the difficulty tiers are honest: the very_hard entries demand real textual knowledge (Nehushtan, Meribah, Seraiah as Jehozadak's father) rather than recognition, and the distractors are chosen to be genuinely tempting. Two limits: it is the smallest bank taken here, and it carries no verse references, so every answer would need its citation added before the questions could be checked or taught from.

uberspot-opentriviaqa.download_method: git clone at that commit, then the religion-faith category file plus LICENSE and README.md copied into raw/ byte for byte. The other 21 categories were not taken, as the brief asked for the religion category only.
uberspot-opentriviaqa.licence_as_stated: CC BY-SA 4.0, stated in README.md, carried in full in the LICENSE file, and detected as CC-BY-SA-4.0 by GitHub's own licence API
uberspot-opentriviaqa.licence_nuance: The cleanest licence statement of any source in this batch, agreed across three places. The honest caveat is upstream: the README says the questions 'were gathered' some years ago from sources it does not name, so the maintainer's CC BY-SA 4.0 covers this collection without establishing that the original questions were his to license. Good enough for a quiz; worth knowing before building anything load-bearing on it.
uberspot-opentriviaqa.attribution_note: Required by CC BY-SA 4.0: credit uberspot/OpenTriviaQA and license any adaptation under the same or a compatible licence.
uberspot-opentriviaqa.questions_written_by_detail: Human-written multiple-choice trivia, gathered rather than authored by the maintainer, with the original writers unrecorded.
uberspot-opentriviaqa.record_unit: one multiple-choice question with its correct answer and the full option list
uberspot-opentriviaqa.format: A plain-text block format: '#Q <question>', then '^ <correct answer>', then one lettered line per option. Apostrophes are stripped throughout the source file.
uberspot-opentriviaqa.publishable_reason: CC BY-SA 4.0 stated in the README and the LICENSE file. Publishable with credit to uberspot/OpenTriviaQA and share-alike on anything built from it.
uberspot-opentriviaqa.usability_note: Publishable with attribution and share-alike, and the largest filtered yield of the three general-knowledge sources at 247 Bible questions.
uberspot-opentriviaqa.quality_note: Solid multiple-choice questions with real distractors, drawn across both testaments and including some that quote the text directly. The category needed heavy filtering rather than trimming: of the questions parsed from religion-faith, only a minority are about the Bible, the rest being Judaism and Jewish history, the modern state of Israel, Catholic devotion to later saints, Buddhism, Scientology, witch trials and, in the very first entry, a film about Casanova. Two quality marks on what was kept: apostrophes are missing throughout ('Bibles interpretation', 'Moses life'), so the text needs repunctuating, and a few answers are 'All of these', which does not survive being shuffled.

Each object is {category_id, lang, tags, question, answer, answers, source}, where 'answer' is an index into 'answers'.

el-cms-open-trivia-database.usability_note: No licence is stated, so it is publishable under the owner's rule of 2026-10-17 for unlicensed public content; the repository's own request to be cited and linked is met by the per-record credit. Its distinctive value is breadth: 300 of its 329 Bible questions were found in a 31,000-record uncategorized pile, so it reaches questions the religion category alone would have missed.
el-cms-open-trivia-database.quality_note: The questions are decent and often specific, but the data is the roughest in the corpus. Every one of the 329 kept records gives the answer alone with no distractors, so despite looking like multiple choice these are open-answer questions and the options field is left empty rather than holding a one-item list. 1,643 of the 31,304 records in the large file, about 5 per cent, carry unescaped double quotes inside their question text and are not valid JSON; 1,599 were recovered by re-escaping, and the remaining 44 were checked individually and hold no Bible question that the filter would have kept. Punctuation and capitalisation are inconsistent throughout ('How many sayings did jesus say from the cross'), and a few kept questions rest on legend rather than text, such as the Last Supper chalice being called the Holy Grail.

opentdb-api.title: Open Trivia Database, Bible questions from the public API
opentdb-api.revision_kind: retrieval date and the session token used, which the API issues to stop repeats within a pull
opentdb-api.download_method: 10 requests to the public API at 50 questions each, one request every 6 seconds against the service's documented limit of one per 5 seconds, using a session token so no question was returned twice and base64 encoding so the text is byte-exact. Each response is kept exactly as returned, one file per request, with a fetch-log.json recording the pull.
opentdb-api.licence_as_stated: CC BY-SA 4.0, as stated by opentdb.com for the Open Trivia Database
opentdb-api.licence_nuance: Clean and unambiguous for the compilation. The questions are submitted by the public and checked by the site's moderators before publication.
opentdb-api.attribution_note: Required by CC BY-SA 4.0: credit the Open Trivia Database (opentdb.com) and license any adaptation under the same or a compatible licence.
opentdb-api.questions_written_by_detail: Submitted by members of the public and verified by the database's moderators.
opentdb-api.record_unit: one question with its correct answer and, for multiple-choice entries, its wrong answers
opentdb-api.format: JSON API responses of {response_code, results}, each result holding category, type, difficulty, question, correct_answer and incorrect_answers, all base64 encoded. Options are listed alphabetically in the extraction because the API returns the correct answer separately from the wrong ones, so the published order is not an order any player ever saw.
opentdb-api.publishable_reason: CC BY-SA 4.0 stated by opentdb.com. Publishable with credit to the Open Trivia Database and share-alike on anything built from it.
opentdb-api.usability_note: Publishable with attribution, but the yield is so small that it barely counts as a source: 3 questions. Recorded in full because the brief asked for it and because the negative result is the useful finding.
opentdb-api.quality_note: The questions are fine, being moderator-verified, but there are almost none. The Open Trivia Database has no religion category at all, so the two nearest pools were taken in their entirety: Mythology, which is Greek and Roman rather than biblical, and General Knowledge. 500 questions came back and exactly 3 are about the Bible. Worth noting for anyone repeating this: the count endpoint advertised 71 Mythology and 469 General Knowledge questions, but the token-based pull returned 50 and 450, the gap being questions the API holds back from a verified pull. This source is a dead end for Bible material and should not be revisited.

internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.title: Sunday school and Bible question books, 1819-1927 (Internet Archive)
internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.source_url: https://archive.org — 67 separate scanned items, each listed below
internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.source_kind: page scans of printed books, with the Internet Archive's machine-read text layer beside them
internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.revision: not applicable — each item is a fixed scan of a fixed printing. The SHA-256 of every file retrieved is recorded below, and each item's own metadata record was saved with it
internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.download_method: the Internet Archive's advanced-search API to find candidates, its metadata API to check each one, and its item-download service to fetch the machine-read text, the page-image PDF and the metadata record for each of the 67. No scraping, no HTML parsing, nothing behind a login — none of the 67 is access-restricted or in the lending collection
internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.licence_as_stated: Public domain in the United States. 32 items are marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT; 17 carry the Library of Congress's statement that it is unaware of any copyright restriction; 1 carries a Creative Commons public-domain mark; the remaining 17 state nothing, which for a pre-1929 American imprint is the ordinary case
internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.git: no — 773 MB of page scans; the PDFs stay on disk, the JSON is committed
internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.copyright_check: Two independent checks, not one. First, the search itself was bounded to items dated 1700-1928, and every item's publication date was then read back out of its own metadata record: they run from 1819 to 1927, the newest being *Know Your Bible?* (W. A. Wilde Company, Boston, 1927). Anything published before 1929 is in the public domain in the United States with no further condition, which is the whole test. One item of the 67, *Intermediate Bible Narratives* from the Lutheran Book Concern, carries no exact year: its catalogue date is `[190-?]`, the librarian's notation for a book known to be from the 1900s without a printed date. Any year in that decade passes the test, so it is kept, but it is the one item whose date is an inference rather than a record. Second, each item's copyright field was recorded as the Internet Archive states it, and every item was checked for access restriction — none is restricted, which is itself a signal, because the Archive locks down the scans it believes are still in copyright. One item needed a closer look: *Bible Quiz Book* is catalogued as January 1920 but attributed to Baker Book House, a publisher not founded until 1939, so the date on the catalogue record cannot be right for that imprint. It is kept, the discrepancy is recorded here rather than buried, and it is the one item in the batch whose date would need confirming from the title page before anything from it ships.
internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.licence_nuance: There is no licence here to interpret: these works are out of copyright and the Internet Archive adds no terms of its own to a public-domain scan. The only courtesy owed is a credit to the library that paid for the scanning, which the per-book table records. The real constraint is the text, not the terms — see the quality note.
internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.format: Per book: the machine-read text (`<id>_djvu.txt`), the page-image PDF, and the Internet Archive's own metadata record saved as JSON so the provenance travels with the files. The extraction reads only the text; the PDF is kept so any question can be checked against the page it was printed on.
internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.quality_note: This is machine-read text off nineteenth-century paper, and that is the thing to understand before using any of it. Three shapes of question book appear — question-and-answer pairs, numbered questions, and bare interrogatives — and each book was tried against all three with the best result kept; the per-book table records which shape won and what share of candidates survived the quality gate. That gate is deliberately strict: a candidate must open with an interrogative or imperative, end in a question mark, run 20 to 400 characters, carry no character that does not belong in English prose, and contain at most two stray single letters. Across the batch it threw out about a third of what the patterns matched. The commonest fault the scanner makes is reading a question mark as a 1, 7, l, I, P or ^, which welds two questions into one unusable record; those are put back where the surrounding shape is unmistakable, and the count of recoveries is recorded per book. What survives reads cleanly in sampling, but individual words are still misread here and there — *heing* for *being*, *togetiier* for *together*. **Nothing from this source should go in front of a reader until it has been checked against the page image.** That is what the PDFs are for, and why the page number is carried on 75% of the records.
internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.publishable_reason: Published before 1929 in the United States, so public domain. Publishable; no obligation attached. Courtesy credit to the scanning library and the Internet Archive. The constraint on this source is the quality of the machine-read text, not its terms.
internet-archive-sunday-school-question-.usability_note: Nobody holds rights in these texts. The Internet Archive adds no licence of its own to a public-domain scan, and 49 of the 67 items carry either an explicit NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT marking or the Library of Congress's statement that it knows of no copyright restriction; the rest are silent, which for a pre-1929 American imprint is the ordinary case rather than a doubt. Courtesy, not law, suggests crediting the scanning library. THE REAL CONSTRAINT IS NOT THE LICENCE BUT THE TEXT: this is machine-read text off nineteenth-century paper, so a share of every bank carries misread words. Nothing here should go in front of a reader until it has been checked against the page image, which is why the scan is kept beside the text.

gutenberg-sunday-school-question-books.title: Sunday school and catechism question books, 1692-1914 (Project Gutenberg)
gutenberg-sunday-school-question-books.source_kind: human transcriptions of printed books, not scans
gutenberg-sunday-school-question-books.revision: Project Gutenberg does not version its texts; the plain-text file and the RDF metadata record for each ebook were taken together on the retrieval date, and the SHA-256 of both is recorded below
gutenberg-sunday-school-question-books.download_method: the full Gutenberg catalogue (`pg_catalog.csv.gz`) was downloaded and searched offline, then each kept ebook was fetched from `gutenberg.org/cache/epub/<n>/pg<n>.txt` with its RDF metadata record
gutenberg-sunday-school-question-books.licence_as_stated: Public domain in the United States — Project Gutenberg hosts nothing else. All eight works were published between 1692 and 1914.
gutenberg-sunday-school-question-books.git: yes — 3.1 MB of text and metadata, small enough to commit
gutenberg-sunday-school-question-books.copyright_check: Project Gutenberg's whole premise is that it distributes only works in the US public domain, and each ebook's RDF record was saved alongside its text. Publication dates run 1692 to 1914, all comfortably before 1929. One candidate failed this test and was dropped: ebook 1670, *Luther's Little Instruction Book*, is a 1994 translation of a 1529 catechism — the underlying work is ancient but that English rendering of it is modern, and it is not what the brief asked for.
gutenberg-sunday-school-question-books.licence_nuance: Project Gutenberg asks that its trademark not be used once its boilerplate is stripped, which is exactly what the extraction does — the text is cut at the START and END markers before anything is parsed, so no Gutenberg licence text reaches the extraction. So credit the book, not Project Gutenberg. This is the same conclusion job 412 reached for the Baltimore Catechism, and it is applied here for consistency. Readers outside the United States should check their own country's term of copyright, as the Gutenberg header warns.
gutenberg-sunday-school-question-books.format: Per book: the plain-text transcription (`pg<n>.txt`) and the Gutenberg RDF metadata record (`pg<n>-metadata.rdf`), matching the naming job 412 used for the Baltimore Catechism. Each book has its own small parser, because a transcription has a reliable printed shape that a scan does not.
gutenberg-sunday-school-question-books.quality_note: Far cleaner than the scans, and the reason this source is worth having despite being a fifteenth the size: these are human transcriptions, so the text needs no proofreading pass, and 4,994 of the 6,125 questions arrive with the answer the book printed. Two books stand out. **Hurlbut's Bible Lessons for Boys and Girls** (1903) is the closest thing in the whole corpus to what the brief described — story-comprehension questions on the Bible narrative, grouped by lesson, each with its answer. **Bible Readings for the Home Circle** (1914) answers every one of its 2,520 questions with a quoted scripture and its reference, which is where 1,901 of this batch's references come from; its doctrinal slant is Seventh-day Adventist and shows in which topics it chooses to cover. Two transcription quirks were dealt with and are worth knowing about. Hurlbut's printed book marks every proper name for pronunciation and the transcription carries those marks as bracketed codes wrapped around the letters themselves, so deleting the brackets deletes the vowels with them; the letter inside each code is kept and the stress marks and syllable hyphens dropped, which turns `J[=e]'sus` back into `Jesus`. About 75 records of 6,125 still carry a stray transcription marker. Three of the eight books print their review questions without answers beside them, the answers being in the exposition above; those 1,127 records have a question and no answer, which is how the book published them.
gutenberg-sunday-school-question-books.publishable_reason: Published before 1929 in the United States, so public domain. Publishable; no obligation attached. Credit the book rather than Project Gutenberg, whose trademark terms apply only to its own boilerplate, which the extraction strips.
gutenberg-sunday-school-question-books.usability_note: Project Gutenberg asks that its trademark not be used once its boilerplate is removed, which is exactly what the extraction does, so credit the book rather than Project Gutenberg - the same conclusion job 412 reached for the Baltimore Catechism. These are human transcriptions, not machine-read scans, so the text is clean and needs no proofreading pass. Readers outside the United States should check their own term of copyright, as the Gutenberg header itself warns.

banks.title: Bible Readings for the Home Circle (Review and Herald, 1914)
